summary:
Kazakhstan does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 104 of the Penal Code, which criminalised "buggery", was repealed in late 1997 and took effect in 1998, introducing a common age of consent of 16, and lesbianism was never a criminal offence. No statute restricts clothing according to gender presentation, and no bathroom or facilities restriction applies to a trans visitor.

A prohibition on LGBT "propaganda" is nonetheless in force. On 30 December 2025 President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law banning "information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation" in public spaces and media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine; the Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. The measure followed a petition titled "We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!", filed by the Union of Parents, which the Ministry of Culture and Information confirmed in June 2024 it was reviewing after the petition met the threshold for government consideration. Human Rights Watch warned on 10 July 2024 that such a ban would violate rights nationwide. Kazakhstan now prohibits LGBTQ propaganda by law alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia, and public advocacy or visible campaigning should be treated as legally exposed.

Legal gender recognition is medicalised, expensive and in practice geographically concentrated. Since 2003 trans people may change the gender marker on identity documents, but only after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder" requiring medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission, at an applicant cost of around ₸100,000 tenge. Since 2023 commissions can in principle be convened in every region; in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty, because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. Since 2011 document changes have required gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation, and people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months, permitting medical transition to begin.

No law protects LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit. Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Bias-motivated violence is documented but thinly investigated. The ILGA-Europe annual review covering January to December 2023 records an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation opened, alongside an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied registration of an employment site after listing its focus. Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE/ODIHR since its 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and is assessed as needing victim-support and awareness measures. ECOM's 2024 analysis identifies health-right barriers for LGBT people in the country alongside informal behavioural practices that formal policy analysis misses.

Social risk persists even where a legal remedy exists. On 24 September 2019 Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who had posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, upholding privacy rights over a "moral foundations" defence; the two women fled the country for eight months fearing for their safety. Police conduct toward trans people is described as unhelpful rather than predatory, with no recorded pattern of police targeting.
tangentialFactors:
The propaganda statute places Kazakhstan alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting "LGBTQ propaganda" by law, and critics of the adoption measure of February 2024, including independent media, noted that it was modelled on Russian legislation. Comparative regional pressure runs in the same direction as the domestic petition movement.

Public opinion is strongly opposed to legal equality: 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage in a 2015-16 Pew survey. That figure predates the current legal regime and is offered as background to the social environment rather than as a current measurement.

Since 2022 a wave of transgender people has arrived from Russia, according to the ILGA-Europe annual review for 2023, which increases the visibility of trans residents and may shape how a trans visitor is received.
localsOnly:
Adoption is closed to same-sex couples. As of 2020 same-sex couples could not legally adopt children, and in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a "key role" in approval, assessed through a "special psychological test".

Gender-marker change carries a medical and financial burden borne by residents rather than short-term visitors: a psychiatric commission evaluation lasting 30 days, medical tests, costs of roughly ₸100,000, and, since 2011, proof of gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation. Regional commissions were authorised in 2023 but only the Almaty commission functions in practice.

Registration refusals on the basis of LGBTQ focus are documented at the level of civil-society administration: an LGBTQI+ education NGO was denied employment-site registration after listing its focus, per the ILGA-Europe review of 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve how the propaganda law signed on 30 December 2025 has been enforced since entry into force, including whether it has been applied to visitors, and no enforcement cases are sourced here.

Hate-crime incidence remains unverifiable from official channels: Kazakhstan has not reported data to the OSCE/ODIHR since 2018 and has no nominated National Point of Contact, so the scale of bias violence is unresolved rather than low.

Whether any medical commission outside Almaty now convenes is stated only as of the source date; the sources do not confirm current regional availability beyond Almaty.

The absence of a general non-discrimination statute is drawn from country coverage that also reports a 2015-16 opinion figure; whether administrative guidance or case law supplies any protection in practice is not sourced.
